Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Sofia Kim (Redwood SE), Alyssa Rivera (Redwood CSM), Priya Shah (CobaltCare Head of ML), Marcus Lee (CobaltCare Infra), Renee Ortiz (CobaltCare Product), Tom Wu (CobaltCare Security)

Summary (auto): Quick sync on pilot econ. Key points: caching recovered ~28% tokens cost for their query mix, batching reduces per-token cost but hurts 95th pctl latency for mobile-like seq lengths; quantized model (8-bit) looks promising but need regen tests. Next steps captured.

==== Transcript ====
Speaker labels and timestamps: timestamps roughly every 30-45s, occasional mis-attributions and transcription noise:

[00:00] Jordan Patel: hey everyone, thanks for hopping on for the weekly sync. quick roll call?
[00:06] Priya Shah: yeah hi, Priya here. running a little late but on.
[00:09] Marcus Lee: Marcus — infra. all good.
[00:12] Renee Ortiz: Renee, product.
[00:14] Tom Wu: Tom from security. two quick items but I can wait.
[00:17] Sofia Kim: Sofia — SE, I'll drive benchmarks today.
[00:20] Jordan Patel: perfect. we'll go through the spreadsheet Sofia uploaded, the caching runs, and then the latency tradeoffs.

[00:34] Sofia Kim: ok first slide — or first sheet. the pilot spreadsheet link is in the deck, but tl;dr: with prefix caching enabled we saw a 24 to 32% reduction in token consumption on your top 10 queries, depends on cache hit rate. the runs we did used a 70% hit sim for session-aware prompts.
[00:51] Priya Shah: that 70% number, is that realistic? our production sessions have, like, lots of context variance.
[00:56] Sofia Kim: good question. we sampled 1k sessions from your logs (was the sample you provided), and the model-level identical prefixes were ~35% but when we allowed semantically similar prefix reuse via fuzzy match it bumped to ~68%. so 70% is an optimistic but reachable with a small normalization pass.
[01:19] Marcus Lee: what about cache warmup? like first-time users will see cold miss overheads — any data there?
[01:25] Sofia Kim: yes cold miss cost was about 12% higher in initial minutes; we simulated warmup over a day and the amortized saving was that 24–32% range. note we also account for KV storage overhead but it's negligible vs token savings.

[01:49] Renee Ortiz: and does caching change hallucination/QA quality? Priya's worried about state bleed.
[01:55] Sofia Kim: we scoped cache keys to request prefix + user id hashed and added TTLs per session. for the reranker flow we validated on your regen set — precision didn't drop measurably; we saw a tiny uptick in exact-match on QA where repeated context helped. still recommend conservative TTLs for open-ended generation.

[02:16] Jordan Patel: moving to batching, the batch size sweep: tokens/sec/$ improves with larger batches — as expected — but p95 latency for short sequences degrades. Sofia, can you quote numbers?
[02:27] Sofia Kim: sure. for your median query (seq len ~120 tokens) tokens/sec/$ at batch 1 is baseline. batch 2 improves tokens/sec/$ by ~18%, batch 4 by ~36%. however p95 tail latency: batch1 ~420ms, batch2 ~650ms, batch4 ~1.1s for that slice. when we limited to 256 max tokens, numbers shifted slightly but same tradeoff.
[02:54] Priya Shah: for mobile app use we need p95 < 600ms generally, so batch 4 is out for the mobile route. but for web/workflow async jobs batch4 looks attractive.
[03:07] Marcus Lee: can we do dynamic batching—route mobile to lower batch or dedicated warm pool?
[03:11] Sofia Kim: exactly. Redwood supports policy-based routing: you can set latency SLO per route and route mobile traffic to low-latency pool (smaller batch sizes, pinned instances) and background jobs to higher throughput pool.

[03:28] Jordan Patel: pricing — we modeled hosted vs dedicated for both pools. initial delta for dedicated reserve is around 35% lower tokens/sec cost at committed utilization assumptions but has commit and minimums. Jordan: (note: I misspoke) — Jordan here — I'll share the sheet.
[03:45] Priya Shah: can you push that delta with burst policy included? we may need spikes.
[03:49] Jordan Patel: yes I'll include burst pricing. also there's an autoscale buffer cost for idle vs burst — I'll annotate.

[04:05] Tom Wu: security question — caching of prefixes, where does KV live? is that customer-managed? we need to know encryption and access control.
[04:12] Sofia Kim: good one. options: Redwood-managed KV in our private tenancy (encrypted at rest) or customer-provided KV over the VPC peering with your HSM/KMS. for the pilot we used Redwood-managed but we can flip to customer-managed for the on-prem path.
[04:28] Tom Wu: and audit logs for token access?
[04:30] Alyssa Rivera: Alyssa chiming in — audit logs are available per request with an option to ship to your SIEM. we have SOC2 controls documented; will share the security pack.
[04:41] Tom Wu: ok please share. also need to confirm KMS integration shape.

[05:00] Sofia Kim: back to rand: we also ran a quantization A/B — 8-bit weight quant produced ~1.12x token/sec improvement and cost drop but small quality delta on a subset of heavy generative prompts. i flagged a few failure cases in the spreadsheet under the "regen-fails" tab.
[05:22] Priya Shah: hmm we can't tolerate regen failures on clinical QA; what's your recommendation?
[05:27] Sofia Kim: for critical QA routes keep full float model, use quantized for non-critical or reranker/pre-filter tasks. or run a parallel verification pass: quantized primary, float regen for flagged low-confidence outputs. that increases cost but protects quality.
[05:44] Marcus Lee: what's the memory footprint difference? will dedicated nodes need larger GPUs?
[05:48] Sofia Kim: quant reduces memory, actually; 8-bit allows denser packing so you may fit more replicas per GPU. that said it depends on sequence length and KV cache memory — we can share exact residency numbers for your model size.
[06:03] Jordan Patel: can we talk about the real-world numbers from your instrumented pilot? Sofia, what's tokens/sec/$ for the mixed workload we ran?
[06:10] Sofia Kim: aggregated mixed workload (50% short, 30% med, 20% long): hosted baseline tokens/sec/$ = 1.0 (normalized), with caching + batch2 = 1.28, caching + batch4 = 1.52. dedicated estimated at 1.9 for batch4 at 80% commit utilization.
[06:33] Renee Ortiz: so practically if we move to dedicated for background scoring only we could save 35–40% on those jobs?
[06:39] Jordan Patel: yes that's a fair read. background scoring tends to be more batch-friendly so dedicated shines.
[06:44] Priya Shah: i want to be skeptical — did you account for regen due to hallucination when using cache? that could increase token usage downstream.
[06:51] Sofia Kim: we measured regen rate on the 500-case regen harness. cached runs did not significantly increase regen; in fact in some cases regen calls went down because repeated context helped the model settle on correct entities. but we flagged outliers.
[07:09] Marcus Lee: network egress costs when using VPC-provided KV — did you model that?
[07:14] Jordan Patel: short answer: yes. Marcus, we included per-call egress approx. it's small relative to token ops but material if your KV is in a different region. we'll put a regional map in the sheet.
[07:27] Tom Wu: also need to ensure logs containing PII are redacted before leaving our VPC.
[07:31] Alyssa Rivera: that's standard — we offer token scrubbing and can configure redaction rules; we'll share config examples.

[07:50] Sofia Kim: quick demo clip I ran earlier shows p95 tail shifting when batch increases; I dropped the video in the drive and timestamped the runs. the important bit is: for mobile route you want target batch <=2. for backend workers batch 4 or 8 depending on throughput.
[08:09] Priya Shah: do we have a recommended split: percent of keys to send to low-latency pool vs high-throughput?
[08:15] Sofia Kim: recommended default for you: route 85% mobile interactive to low-latency pool, 15% background to throughput pool to start; as you collect telemetry we can tune.
[08:24] Renee Ortiz: can we do a canary for 5% of traffic to test quantized flow?
[08:28] Sofia Kim: yes canary is supported — Redwood console supports traffic weights and automatic rollback based on quality/regression alerts.

[08:42] Jordan Patel: scoreboard: caching helps, batching helps cost but hurts latency, quantization helpful but needs careful QA. next steps are the latency sweeps and network/VPC setup. any blockers?
[08:53] Priya Shah: just the KMS answers and a small legal note but not a blocker for bench.
[08:57] Tom Wu: i'll circulate the KMS/HSM spec by Friday.
[09:00] Marcus Lee: I'll open a ticket to provision VPC tunnel and share IPs by Monday.
[09:04] Renee Ortiz: product wants the cost-per-action line item in the sheet — can you add that Jordan?
[09:08] Jordan Patel: yes will add cost-per-action and a simple dashboard slice for product to chew on.

[09:21] Sofia Kim: small note — we noticed one workload where batch2 actually increased latency due to scheduling jitter on the host; we flagged host-level affinity to reduce jitter. Marcus we'll need to coordinate on that.
[09:34] Marcus Lee: noted. we'll try to pin the process for those instances.

[09:40] Priya Shah: i want to capture success criteria: for pilot go/no-go we need top-line: mobile p95 < 600ms 95% of time, overall tokens/sec/$ >= 1.3 after caching, and no critical regen failures on the clinical flows.
[09:55] Jordan Patel: good success criteria — we'll bake that into the pilot doc and track.

[10:02] Alyssa Rivera: i'll follow up with the security pack and SOC2 docs.
[10:06] Jordan Patel: ok last thing, next call cadence — same time next week?
[10:10] Priya Shah: works for us.
[10:12] Renee Ortiz: yes.
[10:14] Jordan Patel: awesome. thanks everyone — will record action items in the CRM and share updated sheets.
[10:18] (end)
